Fides Quaerens Intellectum
FEE-des KWEH-rens in-TEL-ek-toom
Latin theological axiom (Reformed epistemology)
Latin fides (faith, trust) + quaerens (seeking, present participle of quaerere, to seek) + intellectum (understanding, accusative of intellectus); the phrase was used by Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) as the subtitle for his Proslogion (1078), itself an expansion of Augustine's Latin rendering of Isaiah 7:9 LXX: crede ut intelligas (believe in order to understand); the principle is Augustinian and Reformation before it is medieval

Biblical Definition

“Faith seeking understanding” is the patristic and Reformed axiom that faith is not the enemy of reason but reason's proper starting point. Proverbs 1:7 stakes this claim from the beginning: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.” Wisdom does not precede reverence for God; reverence is the epistemological precondition of wisdom. Hebrews 11:3 makes the same movement in the New Testament: “By faith we understand that the worlds were prepared by the word of God.” The order is decisive — faith first, understanding through. Isaiah 7:9 in the Septuagint tradition carried the same logic: if you will not believe, you will not understand. Anselm's formula in the Proslogion is a careful exposition of this scriptural order applied to the philosophical task: he was not attempting to prove God's existence to a skeptic from a neutral vantage point but to help the believing mind comprehend what it already knows by covenant grace. The formula does not subordinate the intellect to sentiment or make reason the enemy of faith; it insists that unregenerate reason operating autonomously from God produces not wisdom but the folly of suppressed truth. The Reformed tradition from Calvin's sensus divinitatis through Van Til's presuppositionalism has consistently maintained that every created mind is bound to begin with God's revelation rather than with autonomous human rationality. Every true act of understanding is an act of faith already at work.

Webster 1828 Definition

FIDES QUAERENS INTELLECTUM: Latin axiom meaning “faith seeking understanding”; the epistemological principle, rooted in Augustine and Anselm and honored by the Reformed tradition, that faith in the God who has spoken is the proper ground from which human understanding proceeds rather than a conclusion to which neutral reason must first lead.

FIDES QUAERENS INTELLECTUM. Latin. Faith seeking understanding. The axiom credited to Anselm of Canterbury's Proslogion (1078), but rooted in Augustine (Sermon 43: crede ut intelligas — believe in order that you may understand) and in the Septuagint rendering of Isaiah 7:9.

The axiom names the proper epistemological order: reverence for God as LORD precedes the exercise of human reason in its highest capacity. Proverbs 1:7 names this the beginning of knowledge; Ps 111:10 calls it the beginning of wisdom. The unregenerate mind that demands neutrality before it will believe has already corrupted the instrument of knowing.

Anselm's Proslogion (1078) employs the method explicitly: it is not addressed to skeptics demanding proof but to a believer meditating on what he already receives by faith. The ontological argument it contains is an act of meditation, not an apologetic concession to the autonomous questioner.

In the Reformed tradition, the axiom grounds both the classical Christian education project (Kuyper: every square inch of the creation under Christ's lordship, understood from faith) and the presuppositional apologetic tradition (Van Til: all reasoning presupposes God's revelation; neutrality is impossible and itself a religious claim).

Key Scripture

Prov 1:7 — "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction."

Heb 11:3 — "Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear."

Isa 7:9 — "And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah's son. If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established."

Ps 111:10 — "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever."

Modern Corruption

Enlightenment rationalism inverted the axiom, demanding that reason first establish the credibility of faith before faith can be received; postmodern theology dissolves fides into communal interpretation with no objective truth to seek.

expand to see more

The Enlightenment's epistemological revolution — descending through Descartes, Locke, Kant, and Hume — reversed the axiom into its opposite: reason must now validate faith from a declared neutral standpoint before faith can be warranted. Scripture must pass the bar of historical criticism, miracles must satisfy Humean probability standards, and theology must earn its place before the tribunal of autonomous reason. This inversion produces not wisdom but idolatry: the creature's reason sits in judgment on the Creator's revelation. The Reformed tradition names this as the philosophical expression of the Fall. The presuppositional tradition (Van Til, Bahnsen, Frame) takes the axiom in its original direction: all human reasoning already operates within a worldview covenantally submitted to God's revelation or in suppression of it (Rom 1:18–21); there is no neutral starting point from which to evaluate God's claims.

Liberal Protestant theology and post-conservative evangelicalism (Stanley Grenz, Brian McLaren) dissolved fides into a community's interpretive practices rather than personal trust in revealed truth. On this account, “faith seeking understanding” becomes a community seeking its own narrative coherence rather than a soul comprehending objective divine revelation. The result is a fides without content — trust in nothing in particular, seeking no determinate truth — because propositional revelation has been reclassified as an Enlightenment artifact. The antidote is the axiom in its full Augustinian sense: faith is covenantal trust in the personal God who has spoken, seeking to understand what He has said and bounded by what He has revealed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin fides (faith/trust), quaerens (seeking), intellectum (understanding); Anselm of Canterbury's Proslogion (1078) gave it classic form; the root principle derives from Augustine's crede ut intelligas (believe in order to understand), which expands the Septuagint rendering of Isaiah 7:9.

expand to see more

Latin fides — faith, trust, confidence; in the New Testament from Greek pistis (πíστιζ): covenantal trust of the soul in the God who has revealed Himself; not mere intellectual assent but personal commitment resting on testimony and pledged by covenant grace

Latin quaerens — seeking, from quaerere (to seek, inquire, investigate); the present participle insists that faith is active, not passive: it asks, probes, tests, and progressively deepens its comprehension of what it already holds by grace

Latin intellectum — understanding, comprehension, from intelligere (to perceive, understand); the goal is not blank new information from outside faith but a deepened grasp of what covenantal knowledge already holds, now pursued with every faculty of the redeemed mind

Augustine of Hippo, Sermon 43 (c. 400 AD) — crede ut intelligas: believe in order that you may understand; Augustine's Latin paraphrase of Isaiah 7:9 in the Septuagint and Vulgate tradition; the direct precursor and source of Anselm's later formula

Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), Proslogion (1078) — originally titled Fides Quaerens Intellectum; a meditation by a believer on what he already receives by faith rather than an apologetic addressed to skeptics; the ontological argument it contains is an act of believing comprehension, not neutral-reason proof

Usage

"Preaching must reclaim the epistemological order the axiom names: not “prove God first, then perhaps trust Him” but “trust God, and from that trust begin to understand His works and ways.” The Proverbs 1:7 rule is a pedagogical principle: the student who comes to learning in the fear of the LORD is already in a posture to receive wisdom, while the student who demands neutrality has already corrupted the instrument of inquiry. The preacher's task is to call unregenerate hearers not to a neutral evaluation of evidence but to the covenantal submission from which true knowledge flows."

"Van Til's presuppositionalism is the 20th-century rigorous development of the axiom applied to apologetics: all reasoning presupposes something — either the self-attesting God of Scripture or some substitute ultimate authority. The Christian apologist does not grant the unbeliever's claimed neutrality but traces every system of thought to its presuppositions, demonstrating that only the Christian system can account for the intelligibility of the world. This is fides quaerens intellectum wielded apologetically: faith pursuing the intellectual defeat of every argument set against the knowledge of God (2 Cor 10:5)."

"Classical Christian education grounds its curriculum in the axiom: the school or university does not begin with a neutral body of knowledge and then add biblical content, but begins with the fear of the LORD as the organizing principle of all inquiry. Mathematics, history, literature, natural science — all are creatures of God, studied under His lordship, interpreted through His Word. Fides quaerens intellectum is not a medieval relic but the epistemological charter of every genuinely Christian educational institution."
